Instructions

Section titled “Instructions”
  • This quiz covers 0.1 Compounding and the Time Value of Money to 0.5 Regression. It is worth 100 points and should take about 120 minutes; each question shows its points.
  • You may use a calculator or code, but do not look at the lessons. The formulas you need are in the formula sheet below.
  • Show your working in calculation questions. Points are given for the working and the reasons; parts with only an answer and no working get no points. A true / false answer without a reason gets no points.
  • Write your answers on paper (or type them). When you are done, click “Copy scoring prompt” at the bottom of the page and send it with your answers to your AI assistant. You can also submit in several parts.

Formula sheet

Section titled “Formula sheet”

Time value of money

  • Future and present value: FV=PV(1+r)nFV = PV(1+r)^nFV=PV(1+r)n, PV=FV(1+r)nPV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}PV=(1+r)nFV​; effective annual rate: EAR=(1+rm)m−1\text{EAR} = \left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^m - 1EAR=(1+mr​)m−1
  • Annuity (payments at the end of each period): PV=Cr[1−(1+r)−n]PV = \frac{C}{r}\left[1 - (1+r)^{-n}\right]PV=rC​[1−(1+r)−n], FV=C (1+r)n−1rFV = C\,\frac{(1+r)^n - 1}{r}FV=Cr(1+r)n−1​
  • Perpetuity (payments at the end of each period): PV=CrPV = \frac{C}{r}PV=rC​
  • Log return: r=ln⁡(1+R)r = \ln(1 + R)r=ln(1+R)

Optimization

  • First-order condition: f′(x∗)=0f'(x^*) = 0f′(x∗)=0; second-order condition: f′′(x∗)<0f''(x^*) < 0f′′(x∗)<0 for a maximum, f′′(x∗)>0f''(x^*) > 0f′′(x∗)>0 for a minimum
  • Lagrangian: L=U(x,y)+λ (M−pxx−pyy)\mathcal{L} = U(x, y) + \lambda\,(M - p_x x - p_y y)L=U(x,y)+λ(M−px​x−py​y)

Questions

Section titled “Questions”
Part 1. True or false

Answer true or false, and give your reason. An answer without a reason gets no points.

Question 1 6 points
The yearly return of fund A has a standard deviation of 25%, and that of fund B 10%. The correlation between them is positive (less than 1). If an investor who holds only B moves part of the money into the more volatile A, the standard deviation of the portfolio must be higher than 10%.
Question 2 5 points
A consumer chooses two goods at prices pxp_xpx​, pyp_ypy​ with budget MMM. More is better, the optimum is interior (the consumer buys both), and the Lagrange multiplier is λ\lambdaλ. If both prices and the budget double, the optimal x∗x^*x∗, y∗y^*y∗ do not change, but λ\lambdaλ becomes half as large.
Question 3 8 points
The expected simple return of an asset is 0 each year. Years are independent with the same distribution, and the return varies from year to year. If the asset is held for a long time, the probability that wealth ends below the initial investment is close to 50%.
Question 4 6 points
The monthly log returns of an index over the past 20 years are independent with the same distribution. Estimating the mean yearly log return from these 240 monthly returns gives the same standard error (computed with the true standard deviation) as estimating it from the 20 yearly log returns: there are 12 times as many observations, but the estimate is no more precise.
Part 2. Problems
Question 5 14 points
A furniture store sells a sofa at a list price of 12,000 dollars. There are two ways to pay. The first is to pay cash today with a 5% discount, that is, 11,400 dollars. The second is a "zero-interest installment plan": no discount, 12 monthly payments of 1,000 dollars at the end of each month, the first one month from now.

You already have enough money in a savings account with a nominal annual rate of 4.8%, compounded monthly. With the installment plan, the money not yet paid stays in the account and keeps earning interest.

(a) Which way of paying is better for you? Explain why you cannot compare 11,400 dollars with 12,000 dollars directly. (5 points)

(b) The salesperson says: "The only cost of the installment plan is the 600-dollar discount you give up. That is like borrowing 11,400 dollars and paying 600 dollars of interest in a year, a rate of only 60011,400≈5.26%\frac{600}{11{,}400} \approx 5.26\%11,400600​≈5.26%." Discount the installments to today at a monthly rate of 0.8%, use the result to estimate the effective annual rate actually implied by the installment plan, and explain what is wrong with the salesperson's calculation. (9 points)
Question 6 16 points
The monthly return yyy of a fund is regressed on the monthly market return xxx, with slope b=1.2b = 1.2b=1.2. The standard deviation of the monthly market return is 5%, and that of the fund 7.5%. There is a lot of data, so estimation error can be ignored. The fund manager plans to hold the fund and sell the market index short: for each dollar in the fund, sell hhh dollars of the index short, so the portfolio's monthly return is y−hxy - hxy−hx (ignore trading costs and borrowing fees).

(a) Show that the hhh that minimizes the portfolio variance equals the regression slope bbb. (4 points)

(b) After hedging with h=1.2h = 1.2h=1.2, the manager says: "The portfolio no longer depends on the market, so its risk is almost 0." Find the standard deviation of the hedged portfolio's monthly return, and use R2R^2R2 to explain why the risk is not 0. (12 points)
Question 7 13 points
A food truck sells meals at a busy market. The price per meal ppp is set by the market and does not depend on how much the truck sells. Selling qqq meals a day costs q220\frac{q^2}{20}20q2​ dollars for ingredients and hourly staff. At the start of each month the truck pays a parking permit of 600 dollars, which has been paid and cannot be refunded. On each day it opens, it also pays a stall fee of 50 dollars, however many meals it sells; on days it does not open, it pays nothing. Treat the number of meals as continuous.

A friend says: "The permit and the stall fee do not depend on how many meals are sold, so they do not affect output. So the truck should open whenever the price is above 0 and choose how much to sell by p=MCp = MCp=MC." Is this right? Find the lowest price at which the truck is willing to open, and how many meals a day it sells at that price. (13 points)
Question 8 14 points
Asset A pays 1,000,000 dollars once, in 30 years, with no payments before. Asset B pays 40,000 dollars at the end of every year, starting next year, forever.

(a) A colleague says: "B's payments last forever, much longer than A's 30 years, so when interest rates rise, B loses more value than A." Let the discount rate rise from 4% to 5%. Compute the percentage fall in the value of each asset, judge the statement, and explain why. (8 points)

(b) If the discount rate rises from 2% to 3% instead, does the conclusion change? Explain why. (6 points)
Question 9 18 points
A fund manager's excess return over an index is normally distributed, independent from year to year, with a standard deviation of 8 percentage points. Suppose he really has skill: the true expected excess return is 2 percentage points a year. Investors use his record for a two-sided test at the 5% level of the null hypothesis "the true expected value is 0": the result is significant when ∣t∣>1.96|t| > 1.96∣t∣>1.96. For simplicity, use the true standard deviation of 8 percentage points to compute the standard error. You may compute normal probabilities with code or use: P(Z>0.79)≈0.215P(Z > 0.79) \approx 0.215P(Z>0.79)≈0.215, P(Z>1.17)≈0.121P(Z > 1.17) \approx 0.121P(Z>1.17)≈0.121, P(Z>1.65)≈0.049P(Z > 1.65) \approx 0.049P(Z>1.65)≈0.049, P(Z>1.96)≈0.025P(Z > 1.96) \approx 0.025P(Z>1.96)≈0.025, P(Z>2.75)≈0.003P(Z > 2.75) \approx 0.003P(Z>2.75)≈0.003.

(a) An investor says: "If he really has skill, 10 years of data are enough to detect it; if the result is not significant after 10 years, that shows he has no skill." Find the probability that his 10-year record is significant, and evaluate the statement. (11 points)

(b) At least how many years of record are needed for the probability that his result is significant to reach 50%? (7 points)
